canonical_statement: The study tested whether a bleeding-risk-stratified heparin protocol using higher initial infusion rates in patients without identifiable bleeding risk would shorten time to therapeutic APTT without increasing major bleeding.
The investigators compared two prospectively identified concurrent cohorts rather than randomized treatment groups.
The source population comprised 109 consecutive patients with acute symptomatic proximal deep vein thrombosis diagnosed by objective testing between January 1990 and April 1991 at LDS Hospital.

population.label: Consecutive patients with acute symptomatic proximal DVT

canonical_statement: Proximal DVT was diagnosed by duplex ultrasonography showing noncompressibility of venous segments or by ascending contrast venography.

population.label: Patients with objectively diagnosed proximal DVT
inclusion_criteria: Duplex ultrasonography with noncompressibility of venous segments or ascending contrast venography

canonical_statement: The protocol cohort included 20 patients who participated in a low-molecular-weight-heparin clinical trial and received intravenous unfractionated heparin according to the standardized protocol.

The nonprotocol cohort included 48 patients excluded from the low-molecular-weight-heparin trial for reasons considered unlikely to influence heparin requirements; their heparin was managed by attending and/or resident physicians.

Reasons placing patients in the 48-patient nonprotocol cohort were refusal of consent (24), heparin started before trial-entry evaluation (11), inability to attend 3-month follow-up (8), or contrast-dye allergy (5).
An additional 23 patients were excluded from the nonprotocol cohort because conditions could alter initial heparin management or the anticoagulant effect of heparin.

population.label: Patients excluded from the nonprotocol cohort
exclusion_criteria: Conditions potentially altering physician initial heparin management
Conditions potentially altering heparin anticoagulant effect

canonical_statement: Before protocol heparin, patients were classified as high or low bleeding risk using predefined criteria: recent surgery/trauma, peptic ulcer history, recent thrombotic stroke, platelet count below 150×10^9/L, or other reasons for increased bleeding risk.
Protocol patients received an initial intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus of 5000 U.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that a protocol using higher initial heparin infusions in patients without identifiable bleeding risk decreased the time needed to achieve therapeutic APTT compared with nonprotocol physician management.
The authors noted that comparison of concurrent cohorts could be biased by patient selection or by transfer of protocol methods to nonprotocol physician management.
The study had too few recurrent venous thromboembolic events to determine whether faster therapeutic anticoagulation reduced recurrent VTE.
The small cohort did not provide adequate statistical power to exclude a type II error for the comparison of major bleeding rates (5% vs 4%).
The authors stated that four APTT measurements in the first 24 hours may be impractical and unnecessary for most patients whose first APTT is therapeutic.

The authors attributed protocol success to higher initial dosing in low-bleeding-risk patients, timely initial APTT measurement, graded dose increases for subtherapeutic APTT, and frequent early monitoring.
